parsed.why: The national document and entry regime sets a serious baseline; the state adds birth-sex restroom rules for students through higher education and restricted inmate care. The facility rule is narrower than a general public-facility ban.

National document, screening and custody exposures remain serious, but the state has no current facility ban or criminalisation of facility use. Restrictive youth-care policy, limited state recourse and birth-certificate disclosure add less direct visitor risk.

National border and document restrictions remain; locally, a current care shield, broad discrimination and hate-crime protections, and no listed facility ban provide meaningful operating protections. The protective legal ranking is not proof of enforcement.

The national regime remains a substantial exposure, but local protections include a care shield, broad nondiscrimination and hate-crime laws, no facility ban, and identity-congruent custody and searches. These materially improve the local visitor-facing picture.

The national regime is compounded by a state law barring trans people from opposite-sex multi-occupancy facilities, a universal exposure with no documented working remedy. Sparse local protections and negative policy assessments add to the risk.
